Products, crossings and singular limits

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A limit of products can retain information that the separate limits lose. At a crossing of coordinate axes, a regularized reciprocal is controlled by parity, while a regularized point mass requires a logarithmic subtraction. At a quartic zero, two Taylor coefficients carry the divergent terms. For two moving positive kernels, their separation relative to their width determines whether their product vanishes, converges or grows without bound.

All pairings are complex-linear, and all distributional limits are tested against arbitrary compactly supported smooth functions. We use . The test topology, Definition 1.2 and Proposition 1.2, supplies the finite-derivative criterion for a distribution. The scalar calculus, §§12–13, supplies cutoffs, Taylor's integral formula and the fundamental theorem of calculus. The integration foundations, §§15–16, supply absolute Fubini, dominated convergence and scalar substitution.

For the quartic calculation we use the proved simple-pole integral and finite-part identity in Real zeros and merging poles, Theorem 2.1, (2.6) and (2.8). The branch and all coefficients for the half-plane parameter are computed below. Cauchy kernels and distributional boundary limits, Theorem 4.1, gives the one-dimensional principal-value convention.

Parity at a product of coordinate hyperplanes

For an integer and , let reverse its -th coordinate, and define The operators for distinct coordinates commute. The function is odd in every coordinate.

Lemma 1 (division of the fully odd part). There is a unique smooth function with . It has compact support. If is supported in , so is , and

Proof. The fundamental theorem gives whenever . Apply it successively in the coordinates of . Oddness gives the required zero in each coordinate, and differentiation in another coordinate preserves it. Differentiation under this compact parameter integral proves smoothness of . The mixed derivative of is an average, with signs, of the corresponding derivatives of , so its supremum is no larger.

Off the coordinate hyperplanes the quotient is , and is zero outside the reflected support box. By continuity it is zero there on the hyperplanes as well. This proves compact support. That same dense complement proves uniqueness of a continuous quotient.

Define the product principal value by the concrete formula Lemma 1 bounds this functional by on each fixed support box. Thus it is a distribution of order at most .

Theorem 2 (a symmetric reciprocal at the crossing). For , The same limit holds through nonzero real values of , since the kernel depends only on . Moreover is the iterated, or independently truncated, principal value in all coordinates.

Proof. The kernel is odd in each coordinate. The identity expresses the difference as a sum whose -th term is even in . Each pairs to zero with the kernel by reflection in that coordinate. The integrals are absolute for each fixed positive , so these reflections are legitimate. Hence The fraction is bounded by one and tends to one off the coordinate hyperplanes, whose Lebesgue measure is zero. The majorant is integrable.

For positive truncation parameters , reflections likewise give The right side tends to (P3) when all parameters tend to zero, independently of their rates; dominated convergence also permits successive limits. For this is precisely the usual symmetric principal value. On a product test , Fubini factors (P3) into the product of its one-dimensional principal values. Formula (P3) specifies the distribution on every test, not only on product tests.

Exercise 3 (advanced) — uniqueness of the homogeneous quartic subtractions. Suppose , , satisfy and has a distributional limit as in . Prove that the three are exactly the coefficients in (P7), with .

Solution. Subtract (P7) from the assumed convergent family. The resulting sum of point derivatives has a limit. For each , take a compact smooth test equal to near zero. Its derivatives of degrees zero through two vanish at zero except for its -th derivative, which is one. It isolates times the difference of the two -th coefficients. That difference must remain bounded as . On the ray , it is its value at times . All three exponents are negative, so boundedness forces that value to vanish. The point was arbitrary. The explicit coefficients in (P7) do satisfy (P31), including the zero first-derivative coefficient.
